newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Kuwait says Gulf will never be safe with Saddam.
newsitem.headline: Kuwait says Gulf will never be safe with Saddam.

text.p: Kuwait said on Saturday fresh tensions with former occupier Iraq showed the Gulf region would never be safe with President Saddam Hussein in power and with Baghdad failing to meet Gulf War ceasefire terms.

The small state at the northern head of the Gulf stressed it was not advocating Saddam's overthrow but would discuss possible "future measures" about Iraq with U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry when he visits Kuwait on Sunday.
"The crisis will never be over until Saddam Hussein goes. This cat and mouse game has to stop," Information Minister Sheikh Saud Nasser al-Saud al-Sabah told a news conference.
"We would like to see, once and for all, an end to this regime sooner rather than later...Some kind of measures will have to be taken to put an end to this," he added.
Kuwait has made similar statements during the periodic security flare-ups it has had with Iraq since the 1991 Gulf War ended a seven-month Iraqi occupation.
Asked if he was directly advocating Saddam's overthrow, Sheikh Saud replied: "I don't think I am in a position to advocate anything.
"We are in a position to discuss this and consult with our allies as to in future what needs to be done with regard to this whole crisis which has been with us since 1990."
He said there was an international consensus that Saddam was a threat to the region.
With most regional allies unwilling to take part in the current U.S. military buildup, Washington is dispatching added warships to the region and 5,000 troops to Kuwait.
Eight Stealth radar-evading bombers landed in Kuwait on Friday as part of preparations for a possible military strike against Iraq.

Sheikh Saud, who was ambassador to Washington during the 1990-91 Gulf crisis, said Kuwait had taken all immediate and necessary security measures. "We will never be caught unprepared again. We will take all necessary measures."

He said any critics of Kuwait's decision to accept U.S. help had to remember that Kuwait is a small country bordered by a larger, more powerful state with a history of aggressive behaviour towards neighbours.

Sheikh Saud predicted any military action against Iraq would not split the Gulf War multinational coalition, adding that media reports of disagreements between major powers and even between Kuwait's Gulf Arab allies over Iraq had been exaggerated.

Commenting on an Iraqi pledge on Friday evening to respect an expanded no-fly zone in southern Iraq, Sheikh Saud said Iraq had shown it could change its mind, occasionally respecting the zone and then attacking Western planes overflying the area.
"We should not let Saddam Hussien off the hook on such issues," he said.
"We are not just discussing side issues like no-fly zones. There are major issues we are talking about here, mainly the full implementation of U.N. Security Council resolution 687."

The April 1991 resolution established the ceasefire, guaranteed the inviolability of the Iraq-Kuwait border, set up U.N. observer forces on the border, launched the dismantling of Iraqi weapons of mass destruction, set terms for war damage compensation and provided a framework for an eventual easing of sanctions imposed against Iraq since 1990.
